title: Who I am
job: Introduce yourself and state what you like
verifiedBy: Fable (Claude Fable 5) — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: Nothing in this module moves out of the order you already think in: ismī Rohān, uḥibb al-qahwa. (Written Arabic can put the verb before a spelled-out subject noun; no sentence here has one.)

In the present, a statement that starts with a noun or a pronoun has no "to be" at all: ismī Rohān is "my-name Rohan" and it is a whole sentence. This is the present affirmative only — the past has kāna (M5), and the present negative needs laysa, which L1 never teaches.

The person lives inside the verb, on the front: u- is I (uḥibb, urīd), tu- is you or she (tuḥibb), ya- is he (yuḥibb). So a sentence with a verb needs no pronoun, and anā uḥibb reads as emphasis — "I'm the one who likes it" — rather than as neutral speech.
Where there is no verb, the pronoun is obligatory: anā min al-Hind. Nothing else in that sentence can say who is being talked about.

Possession is a suffix, not a word. ism (name) + -ī = ismī (my name); the same tail gives ismuka (your, to a man), ismuki (your, to a woman), ismuhu (his). M7 will hang the same endings on ʿind- to say "I have".

al- ("the") is written onto the front of its noun with a hyphen and is part of that word: al-Hind, al-qahwa. It is never a separate word the way English "the" is, and in M2 it changes shape before certain letters.
A general statement KEEPS al- where English drops it: uḥibb al-qahwa is "I like coffee" — coffee as a whole class of thing. uḥibb qahwa sounds like "I like a coffee", one cup.
A request DROPS al- where English would keep it: urīd qahwa, urīd māʾ. Put al- back and you are pointing at one particular thing — urīd al-māʾ is "I want THE water", that glass on the table.

A word that describes someone follows the SUBJECT of the sentence, not the person speaking: anā ṭālib from a man, anā ṭāliba from a woman — and Rohān ṭālib, Priyā ṭāliba, whoever says them. The -a marks the person being described as female.

words.note: ism is "name"; the -ī on the end is "my". Possession is a suffix, not a word: ismuka (your name, to a man) · ismuki (to a woman) · ismuhu (his name).
Names carry over — Arabic spells them out by sound. Swap in your own.

sentences.trap: English needs "is" and Arabic has nothing to put there. ismī Rohān is already the whole sentence.
sentences.sound: ISS-mee ro-HAAN — hold the s, and the -ī is a long ee.

variations.changed: swap the name — ismī itself never changes
-ī (my) → -uhu (his): the owner hangs off the end of the word

variations.cue: Your name is Rohan (to a man)
variations.changed: -ī (my) → -uka (your, to a man): the same tail, turned on the listener

mistake.why: huwa ("he/it") is the English "is" smuggled in. The present tense has no copula: ismī Rohān.

sentences.usage: First introductions, spoken or written, any register.
sentences.mnemonic: ismī = "name-my". The owner comes last, stuck to the end.

words.note: "I" — obligatory here, because this sentence has no verb to carry the person. Beside a verb it would be emphasis instead (uḥibb, not anā uḥibb). M2 fills the same slot with anta and anti ("you", male and female).
Works like English "from" and sits where English puts it.

al- is the definite article, "the", written onto the front of its noun with a hyphen — al-Hind, al-qahwa, al-māʾ. It belongs to the word, not beside it. Country names carry it even where English drops it, so "from India" is min al-Hind. (Before some letters al- changes shape — that is M2.)

sentences.trap: English says "from India" bare. Arabic keeps the article: min al-Hind, never min Hind.
sentences.sound: a-NAA min al-HIND — the al- runs straight onto the noun, said in one breath.

variations.changed: swap the country — Miṣr is one of the few that takes no al-
a name instead of anā — still nothing where English puts "is"
who and where-from in one verbless line — anā carries both halves

mistake.why: The article is not optional on this noun. It is min al-Hind.

sentences.usage: Where you are from — the second line of nearly every introduction.
sentences.mnemonic: Arabic says "the India": the article is glued on, al-Hind.

words.note: ṭālib describes a male student, ṭāliba a female one — the -a follows whoever the sentence is about, not whoever is speaking. Bare, with no word for "a" in front of it: Arabic has no indefinite article.

sentences.trap: There is no word for "a". "I am a student" is two words in Arabic, and both of them are already there.
sentences.sound: ṭ is a heavy t said with the tongue low and the mouth wide: TAA-lib.

variations.cue: I am a student (said by a woman)
variations.changed: add -a — the description follows the person described
a name in the subject slot, and still no "is"

variations.cue: My name is Rohan and I am a student
variations.changed: two verbless statements joined by wa — the introduction grows a second half

mistake.why: wāḥid is the number one, not the English "a". Arabic has no indefinite article at all: anā ṭālib.

sentences.usage: Saying what you do or what you are — student, teacher, engineer.
sentences.mnemonic: ṭālib is one who seeks (ṭalab = to seek) — a student seeks knowledge.

words.note: saʿīd of a man, saʿīda of a woman — same -a as ṭālib/ṭāliba, and it tracks the subject of the sentence. An adjective needs no "am" in front of it either.

sentences.trap: "I am happy" has three words in English and two in Arabic. The "am" has nowhere to go.
sentences.sound: sa-ʿEED — the ʿ is a tightening deep in the throat just before the long ee.

variations.cue: I am happy (said by a woman)
variations.changed: add -a — the adjective follows the person it describes
the adjective describes Rohan now — it follows its subject, not the speaker

variations.cue: I am happy and I like music
variations.changed: wa joins the adjective half to a verb half — one speaker, two statements

mistake.why: Said by a man this is wrong: -a describes a female subject. A man says anā saʿīd.

sentences.usage: How you are, in the moment or in general. Also the polite "pleased to meet you" (anā saʿīd bi-liqāʾik) that L1 does not teach.
sentences.mnemonic: saʿīd is also a man's name — Said, "the happy one".

words.note: One verb does both like and love. The person is the prefix: u- = I, tu- = you (to a man) or she, ya- = he — and spoken to a woman, the tu- verb keeps an -īn tail: tuḥibbīn. So the "I" is already in the word and needs no anā beside it.

qahwa is coffee; al-qahwa is coffee with the article on it. Liking a whole class of thing keeps the article — uḥibb al-qahwa — while asking for some drops it: urīd qahwa. Both shapes are this same word.

sentences.trap: English "I like coffee" has no "the" in it, and Arabic must have one. Leave al- off and you have asked about a single cup.
sentences.sound: u-ḤIBB al-QAH-wa — ḥ is a hard breathy h from the throat, and q is a k made right at the back.

variations.changed: u- → tu-: the prefix is the whole change
u- → ya-: he, and still no pronoun in the sentence
spoken to a woman, tu- is not enough: the verb keeps its -īn tail — tuḥibbīn

mistake.why: Without al- this is "I like a coffee", one cup. Coffee in general is al-qahwa.

sentences.usage: Likes of every kind — drinks, music, people, places.
sentences.mnemonic: ḥubb is love — the same root as ḥabībī, "my love".

words.note: Borrowed from Greek, and it still takes the article like any other Arabic noun: liking music in general is uḥibb al-mūsīqā, exactly as with al-qahwa.

sentences.trap: A word you already recognise still plays by Arabic rules: mūsīqā needs its al- in a general statement.
sentences.sound: moo-SEE-qaa — the q again from the back of the throat, and the last vowel is long.

variations.changed: swap what is liked — the article rides along with it
u- → ya-: the person is the prefix, nothing else moves
u- → tu-: the prefix turns to you, and the sentence still needs no pronoun

mistake.why: The "I" is already the u- on the verb. Adding anā is emphasis — "I'M the one who likes music" — not the plain sentence.

sentences.usage: Everyday likes. The same frame carries any noun you know.
sentences.mnemonic: mūsīqā is the English word with an Arabic coat on: al-mūsīqā.

words.note: The everyday verb for wanting, with the same u- prefix as uḥibb: the "I" is inside it. M3 adds the other persons (turīd, yurīd) and lā urīd for refusing.

sentences.trap: This is the mirror of uḥibb al-qahwa: asking for something drops the article that liking it required.
sentences.sound: u-REED QAH-wa. The final -a of qahwa is short and light.

variations.changed: add al- — now it is that particular coffee, the one already talked about
swap what is wanted — still bare, because it is a request

variations.cue: I want a coffee and water
variations.changed: wa joins the two things wanted — both stay bare, because both are requests

mistake.why: tu- is "you". For "I want", the prefix is u-: urīd qahwa.

sentences.usage: Ordering and asking, in a café or at home. Direct rather than rude; the polite frames come later.
sentences.mnemonic: urīd — "you read" it wrong: the u- at the front means I, not you.

words.note: The ʾ at the end is hamza, a catch in the throat — it is a consonant, so māʾ and mā are different words. Bare māʾ is water in general; al-māʾ is that particular water.

sentences.trap: English "I want water" and "I want the water" are two sentences; in Arabic the difference is the three letters al-.
sentences.sound: maa followed by a tiny stop, as in the middle of "uh-oh" — not a trailing aah.

variations.changed: add al- — that glass, not water in general
want → like, and the article comes back with it

variations.cue: I like coffee and I want water
variations.changed: both laws in one line: al- on the liked class, bare on the thing asked for

mistake.why: Drop the final catch and the word is mā, "what". Water ends on the hamza: māʾ.

sentences.usage: Asking for what you want — a table, a shop, someone's kitchen.
sentences.mnemonic: māʾ ends the way "uh-oh" breaks in the middle: a little stop after the aa.

words.note: "Much", turned into an adverb by the -an on the end, and it goes AFTER what you like: uḥibb al-qahwa kathīran. That -an is one of the few endings this course writes out.

sentences.trap: English can put "really" in front of the verb. Arabic puts kathīran at the end of the sentence.

variations.changed: swap what is liked — kathīran stays at the end
u- → ya-, and the rest of the sentence holds still

variations.cue: You like India a lot (to a man)
variations.changed: u- → tu-: you — and kathīran keeps its seat at the end

mistake.why: kathīran comes after the thing liked, not before it: uḥibb al-Hind kathīran.

sentences.usage: Warming up any liking — food, places, people.
sentences.mnemonic: kathīr = many; add the -an tail and "many" becomes "a lot".

sentences.cue: I am a student and I like music

words.note: "And", joining two statements. In Arabic script it is written stuck to the next word (وأحب); this course spaces it out so that each word stays its own word.

sentences.trap: The second half needs no second "I": uḥibb already carries it, even after wa.
sentences.sound: wa runs straight into whatever follows: wa-u-ḤIBB, with no pause.

variations.cue: I am a student and I like coffee
variations.changed: swap the second half — wa joins whatever comes next

variations.cue: I am a student and I like music (said by a woman)
variations.changed: ṭālib → ṭāliba: only the description of the subject changes

variations.cue: Rohan is a student and likes music
variations.changed: the whole frame in the third person: the name is the subject, and after wa the verb turns to yu- with it

mistake.why: Two statements need wa between them. Without it the sentence reads as "I am a student who likes music".

sentences.usage: The whole introduction in one line — who you are, then what you like.
sentences.mnemonic: wa is the smallest word in the language and it does the same job as "and".

comprehensionPool.cue: I am a student (said by a woman)
I want a coffee and water
